title: What can you say about psyllium husk in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 3 wordings for psyllium husk; the strongest is "Promotes regular bowel movements by adding bulk and water to the stool" (moderate, 2.5-30 g husk a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Relieves or treats constipation, without 'occasional', or anything about chronic constipation".

supported_wordings.wording: Promotes regular bowel movements by adding bulk and water to the stool.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists this use with doses drawn from European, WHO and FDA references; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Adults and adolescents 13-17: 2.5-30 g husk a day, no more than 8 g per dose (seed: 2.5-40 g, no more than 13 g per dose). Children 6-12: 1.25-15 g husk a day, no more than 4 g per dose. Drink at least 250 ml of liquid with each dose. Effects show 12-24 hours after the first dose and may take 2-3 days.
supported_wordings.form: Dry or powdered psyllium husk (or seed at the seed doses), mixed with liquid

supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists constipation relief at these doses; FDA's 2000 rule counts the 'occasional' form as structure-and-function wording.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Same doses and directions as above. Labeling should make clear the product is not meant for chronic constipation.
supported_wordings.form: Dry or powdered psyllium husk (or seed at the seed doses), mixed with liquid

supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Same doses and directions as above. Health Canada words this use as gentle relief of 'constipation and/or irregularity'; this entry keeps only the irregularity wording (see notes).
supported_wordings.form: Dry or powdered psyllium husk (or seed at the seed doses), mixed with liquid

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Relieves or treats constipation, without 'occasional', or anything about chronic constipation
wordings_to_avoid.why: FDA's 2000 rule clears only the 'occasional constipation' form; chronic constipation may be a symptom of serious disease.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Lowers cholesterol, or reduces heart disease risk, outside FDA's authorized wording and conditions
wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a disease. The supported route is FDA's authorized soluble-fiber claim, with its wording and conditions (see fda_health_claims).
Names a disease. FDA lists a qualified claim on psyllium and type 2 diabetes risk, but its wording was not read (see fda_health_claims).

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: FDA final rule on structure/function statements, 65 FR 1000 (6 January 2000), page 1015
FDA authorized health claim: Soluble fiber from psyllium seed husk and reduced risk of coronary heart disease
FDA qualified health claim: Psyllium husk and reduced risk of type 2 diabetes

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
